project_name: University of Puget Sound Courseware System
initial_requirements: The University of Puget Sound needs a courseware system that better supports its instructional and educational practices. Students, professors, and system administrators should be able to manage courses, assignments, learning materials, discussions, and grades through a coherent online environment. The project should also improve collaboration and access to course content while allowing the university to refine the system as stakeholder needs become clearer.

slots.key: Special approval steps for administrative roles and emergency access
slots.value: Special approval would be needed when someone needs elevated access to student records, grading, or account administration outside their normal job role, especially if it is temporary or broad in scope. Emergency access should be limited to situations like an account lockout, a critical course issue right before a deadline, a security incident needing immediate response, an enrollment issue, a time-sensitive grading problem, or a verified emergency where normal permissions would prevent work from getting done. Approval should come from a system administrator, and in some cases also a dean or department chair if the access affects academic records or a whole course section. Approval should not be automatic just because someone asks; there should be a clear reason logged, and the access should expire after the immediate need is over. Requests for account recovery, temporary access, or data correction require identity verification and approval from someone with the right authority for that account type, with more sensitive changes needing a second check from admin staff. If the request is unusual or affects grades, enrollment, or permissions, an extra review is required before it goes through.

slots.key: Peer collaboration space creation, membership, moderation, and access controls
slots.value: Instructors should usually be able to create or approve peer collaboration spaces. Students should only join if they are enrolled in the course or explicitly invited. Moderators may be set by the instructor or by the group itself if that is allowed. Spaces should become read-only after a course ends or if the instructor closes them because the activity is finished or needs moderation. Some spaces should be closed to certain participants when they are for smaller project groups or when a student has been removed from the course. When a participant is moved out of the group or removed from the course, they should lose posting access right away and probably lose viewing access too, unless an instructor decides they need read-only access for a transition period. The space should then be limited to the remaining group members, plus the instructor and any authorized staff who need oversight. Old participants should be prevented from rejoining on their own; any continued access must be explicitly granted.

slots.key: Course roster, assignment, submission, and grade records
slots.value: A course is the overall class offering; a section is a specific instance of that course with its own instructor, schedule, and roster; assignments are anything students are expected to submit or complete for credit (paper, quiz, project, or discussion participation); grades reflect the instructor's evaluation of student performance in that section; feedback is comments or guidance tied to a submission or performance. Instructors should be able to give feedback before grading, after grading, or at the same time. Students should be able to view feedback for their own work, but not other students' unless the instructor explicitly posts it for the class. If an instructor posts feedback by mistake, they should be able to edit it, and changes should be recorded for accountability. Students should be able to view course content, submit assignments, participate in discussions, and see their own grades and feedback. Professors should be able to create and manage course materials, assignments, discussions, and grading for the courses they teach. Enrollment should control access tightly so only officially enrolled students can use the full course tools; waitlisted students should get only temporary limited access during add/drop, such as basic course information and possibly instructor-approved materials, and dropped students should lose access quickly with a short grace period if needed for already-submitted assignments or pending administrative updates. Waitlisted students should not have full participation rights unless they are actually enrolled. The system should follow the official enrollment status, with enough flexibility to avoid disrupting legitimate transitions. Special cases like auditors or accommodations require explicit rules, including exception-based access for approved auditors or disability accommodations, with access limited to the specific materials or tools needed rather than full course access by default, and removed promptly when approval expires or the accommodation changes. slots.key: Retention period for academic records and artifacts
slots.value: Retention must meet institutional requirements; when course materials are updated or replaced, the new version should become visible to students right away in most cases, while the previous version should still be retained by the system as a record of what changed. Older versions should generally not remain visible to students unless the instructor intentionally leaves both available, such as for comparison, assignment history, or when students already used the earlier version for a submission, a class discussion, or a graded activity. The earlier version may also remain visible when the instructor explicitly chooses to keep both versions visible, or when the item is part of the course record and needs to remain available for transparency. Otherwise, the newer version should replace it and the old one should be archived behind the scenes.

slots.key: Academic record privacy and access controls
slots.value: Access to grades and student feedback should be limited by role and course enrollment, and sensitive information should not be broadly visible; the system should support university privacy and academic record practices, including FERPA-related and university policy requirements. Access should be role-based, logged, and limited to what each user needs, with controlled and auditable support for emergency access, account recovery, temporary access, and data correction. Special approval should be required for elevated access to student records, grading, or account administration outside a person's normal job role, especially when the access is temporary or broad in scope. Emergency access should be limited to situations like an account lockout, a critical course issue right before a deadline, or a security incident needing immediate response. Enrollment status should enforce access tightly: only officially enrolled students should have full access, while waitlisted students should have temporary limited access during add/drop and dropped students should lose access quickly, with a short grace period only when needed for already-submitted assignments or pending administrative updates. Exception-based access should be available for approved auditors or disability accommodations, limited to the specific materials or tools needed rather than full course access by default, and removed promptly when approval expires or the accommodation changes. A release must stop immediately if it could expose student records, grades, private discussion content, or instructor materials to the wrong people, including any sign that roles, permissions, or course membership are being enforced incorrectly. If a privacy issue is found in testing or rollout, monitoring should not continue until it is fixed and verified.

slots.key: Student information system synchronization for courses and enrollments
slots.value: The sync should handle mid-term section changes, adds, drops, cancellations, and cross-listed courses carefully so the course roster and student access stay accurate; cross-listed courses should use one shared course roster with the student associated to their specific section behind the scenes to avoid duplicate-looking enrollments while still preserving section-level detail. If a student changes sections, the system should update the section assignment without creating a second enrollment record. If both views are needed, it should be one authoritative enrollment plus section membership, not separate full copies everywhere. For canceled classes, the system should mark the course clearly as canceled and stop normal course activity rather than leaving it in an active state. If a student drops after work has already been submitted, their existing records should be preserved for instructors and administrators even if they lose access to the course.

In the reverse direction, the courseware system may send limited data back, such as course participation or grades, but only if the university decides to use it that way and with very careful control. The exact authoritative fields on each side still need confirmation.

slots.value: If an integration is on a critical path, such as login or grade updates, pause the release if it fails outright or if a data format change could corrupt records or block users. If a critical-path integration fails outright or changes format in a way that could corrupt records or block users, pause the release. If the issue is limited to a noncritical feed and there is a safe manual workaround, proceed temporarily with monitoring while fixing it. If student access, instructional work, or data integrity are at risk and the issue cannot be contained quickly, stop and fall back rather than push ahead. Roster sync and file storage are boundary cases that should be treated very carefully: if roster sync is stale but the current term can still function without serious access problems, continue briefly with monitoring and a manual backup process; if it creates wrong enrollments or blocks course access, stop immediately. File storage is a hard stop if uploads or downloads fail in a way that interrupts assignments or loses content. Notification feeds are less critical unless they are the only way people receive time-sensitive alerts; if the core system still works and notifications can be delayed or sent another way, monitoring may be enough for a short period.

slots.value: Access should be role-based and limited to what each user needs. Requests for account recovery, temporary access, or data correction should require identity verification and approval from someone with the right authority for that account type; more sensitive changes require a second check from admin staff. slots.key: Off-campus access handling and security controls
slots.value: Off-campus access should generally work the same as on-campus for most students and faculty to support use from home or while traveling. Sensitive information should use stronger login controls, and the system may apply extra checks when unusual activity is detected. Extra checks should kick in when the login looks unusual, such as a new device, a different country or region, or a rapid change in location that doesn’t make sense. Access should be tightened for attempts to open sensitive items like exam banks, grade records, or student information from outside the campus network. In those cases, the system should require stronger authentication and may restrict the most sensitive content until the user is verified. Normal academic use off campus should stay easy, but high-risk access should get more scrutiny without making everyday access cumbersome.

slots.key: SIS-to-courseware synchronization data and timing
slots.value: The courseware system should receive the official course catalog, section information, instructor assignments, and student enrollments from the student information system as the source of truth. Enrollment-based access should follow the official enrollment record and enforce the current enrollment status rather than manual exceptions. These updates should happen automatically on a regular basis and also whenever there is a major registration change, such as add/drop periods or roster corrections. During add/drop, waitlisted students may have temporary access to basic course information and possibly materials if the instructor allows it, while access for dropped students should be removed quickly with a short grace period only for already-submitted assignments or pending administrative updates. For in-progress assignments or graded work, a short grace period tied to the next roster sync should prevent abrupt access loss before the update is fully processed. Once the official enrollment change is confirmed, access should be limited promptly and the grace period should be treated as a practical transition window, not an open-ended exception. Mid-term section changes, adds, drops, and cancellations should update cleanly so the course roster and student access stay accurate, and cross-listed courses should share the right sections without duplicating enrollment in a confusing way. For cross-listed courses, use one shared course roster for the cross-listed course, with the student associated to their specific section behind the scenes. If a student changes sections, update the section assignment without creating a second enrollment record. Use one authoritative enrollment plus section membership, not separate full copies everywhere. If a student drops after work has already been submitted, their existing records should be preserved for instructors and administrators even if they lose access to the course. Canceled classes should be marked clearly as canceled and normal course activity should stop rather than leaving the course in an active state.

Growth and capacity headroom expectations
slots.value: Some buffer between terms so the system is not running right at the edge of capacity when enrollment changes or a new term starts; capacity review should be triggered by a noticeable jump, like around 20 percent more courses or active users than the previous term, or by a major integration affecting login, grading, or content delivery. Capacity should also be reviewed when course structure changes create lots of new activity, such as more discussion use, more uploaded media, more frequent automated jobs, adding plagiarism checking, analytics dashboards, notification services, or anything that sends lots of automated messages; major changes in assignment volume, media-heavy courses, or a big shift toward synchronous online activity would also be worth checking. The 20 percent figure is only a rough guideline, not a hard rule; a smaller but risky change can still trigger review, and if the system is already under strain, even a 10 percent increase may warrant looking sooner. slots.key: Acceptance criteria for core courseware workflows
slots.value: Successful if faculty can manage courses more efficiently, students can find materials quickly and keep up with classes more easily, administrators have a reliable system that supports the university's teaching practices, and the platform improves collaboration while reducing confusion about deadlines and course content. At the start of a new term, the system should create fresh course spaces from official course and enrollment data so instructors do not have to rebuild everything manually. When a course is repeated, there should ideally be a way to copy selected materials, templates, or settings from a previous term. If a course continues across terms, it should be handled as either a linked continuation or a new section with some carried-forward content, depending on how the registrar structures it. Old term content should stay separated from new term content unless someone intentionally copies it forward.

slots.value: Receive official course catalog, section information, instructor assignments, and student enrollments from the student information system as the source of truth; updates should happen automatically on a regular basis and whenever there is a major registration change such as add/drop periods or roster corrections.
